name: Sofpironium

lead: Sofpironium is a prescription gel applied to the underarms to reduce excessive sweating, so clothing stays dry and free of visible sweat marks. It was first approved in Japan in September 2020 as Ecclock and is sold in the US as Sofdra for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and children aged 9 and older.

It blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on sweat glands where it is applied, reducing the signal that triggers sweating. Randomized trials have compared the gel with an inactive vehicle gel. It is a medicine for a recognised medical condition rather than a cosmetic.

paras: It is applied to the underarms as directed by a prescriber, as a daily-use topical. People use it for dry shirts and fewer sweat stains, and it only affects the area where it is applied.

Label-listed adverse reactions include dry mouth, blurred vision, dilated pupils, skin irritation and urinary retention. The label also warns about lack of sweating in hot conditions. It is prescription only.

chain: Dry shirts, no visible sweat marks
angle.text: Sofpironium gel stops underarm sweat at the source, so shirts stay dry and sweat marks do not show. It blocks receptors on sweat glands where it is applied. It is a prescription medicine, approved in Japan as Ecclock and in the US as Sofdra, with randomized trial support.

lead: Sofpironium bromide is a topical anticholinergic gel developed by Bodor Laboratories and licensed to Brickell Biotech for primary axillary hyperhidrosis (excessive underarm sweating). It is designed to reduce sweating by blocking M3 muscarinic receptors in eccrine glands at the application site.[1] It received its first approval in Japan in September 2020 under the brand name Ecclock.[1]

In the United States the product is sold as Sofdra, and its label lists the indication as primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and pediatric patients aged 9 years and older.[2] People look at it for appearance because underarm sweat is a grooming and clothing concern, and the gel is a prescription medicine for a recognised medical condition rather than a cosmetic product.
Randomized trials have compared the gel with vehicle (an inactive gel).[3][4] Anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary retention are listed on the US label.[2]

For people whose concern is visible underarm sweat marks on shirts, sofpironium belongs to the class of topical anticholinergics, which are applied to the axilla rather than taken by mouth. It was designed on a retrometabolic principle: the molecule is meant to act on sweat glands where applied and then be rapidly broken down, which its developers pursued to limit effects elsewhere in the body.[5][6]
infobox: Bodor Laboratories; licensed to Brickell Biotech[1]

paras: The US label indicates sofpironium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and children aged 9 and over.[2] A registered phase 2 trial has also examined the gel in palmar (hand) hyperhidrosis.[7]
Sofpironium is a competitive inhibitor of acetylcholine receptors on peripheral tissues, including sweat glands, and so indirectly lowers the rate of sweating.[2]

The label lists the most common adverse reactions (incidence of 2% or more) as dry mouth, blurred vision, application site pain, application site redness, dilated pupils, application site dermatitis, itching, urinary retention and application site irritation.[2] Warnings include urinary retention, the possibility of a generalized lack of sweating in hot environments, and effects on activities such as operating machinery.[2] No human pregnancy data are available; animal reproduction studies at the doses tested showed no significant adverse effects.[2]

A 2025 systematic review of sofpironium bromide covered five studies and 752 patients and reported that the share of patients reaching a Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale (HDSS) score of 1 or 2 ranged from 53.9 to 86.7 percent, with greater falls in gravimetric sweat weight and Dermatology Life Quality Index score in the sofpironium groups; serious adverse events were not observed in the treated groups.[8] A 2026 meta-analysis of five randomised trials with 1,398 participants, 807 of them on sofpironium, found that the gel reduced gravimetric sweat production by about 25 mg compared with vehicle and raised the likelihood of achieving at least a two-point HDSS improvement (risk ratio 3.27, 95 percent CI 1.57 to 6.80).[5] A separate 2026 meta-analysis of eight randomised trials (1,921 participants) of topical anticholinergics, covering glycopyrronium, sofpironium bromide and umeclidinium, also found that the agents outperformed placebo on the HDSS endpoint.[9]

The Drugs 'first approval' review records that the gel was approved in Japan in September 2020 as Ecclock.[1] Its 5% concentration was tested in a Japanese phase 3 trial and a 52-week open-label extension.[3][10] In the United States, the pivotal programme (the Cardigan I and Cardigan II phase 3 studies) tested a 12.45% gel in randomised, double-blind, controlled trials, with pooled results published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in 2025, and the Medical Letter reviewed Sofdra in 2024.[6][11] Registered trials include a paediatric safety study and a palmar hyperhidrosis study.[7][12] A 2022 observational study of 5% gel in Japanese patients looked at earlier effects within two weeks of starting.[13]

A 2022 review summarised recent advances in topical anticholinergic treatment of hyperhidrosis, the drug class that sofpironium joins.[14] Sofpironium is a prescription medicine for a medical diagnosis rather than a consumer deodorant.

A Japanese phase 3, vehicle-controlled trial of 5% sofpironium gel over 6 weeks used a combined primary endpoint of a Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Score of 1 or 2 plus at least a 50% reduction in gravimetric sweat weight.[3] A 52-week open-label extension in Japanese patients assessed longer-term safety and efficacy.[10] A US phase 2 randomized, double-blind trial tested three dosages against vehicle over 42 days.[4] Further phase 3 trials in the US are registered.[12] A 2025 systematic review has summarized efficacy and safety in primary hyperhidrosis.[8]
